title: ASIC turns up heat on cold callers targeting super
full_text:
Advice firms using cold callers are raking in millions of dollars convincing Australians to move their superannuation out of the major funds and into higher-risk options.
Some advisers are even leaving the “advice” component to unlicensed and unqualified cold callers, also known as lead generators, according to the corporate regulator.
A deep dive by the Australian Securities & Investments Commission into this murky segment of the booming financial advice industry found 15 licensees took $9.8m in upfront advice fees from 7639 recruited clients between the start of 2025 and mid-2026, and got these clients to agree to a further $4.5m in annual recurring fees.
All up, $678m was invested following cold-call referrals, with 90 per cent of it coming from super savings. And the lines used by cold callers to convince people to switch were potentially misleading, ASIC warned.
In one instance, a cold caller suggested to a prospective client that “one of the big bank funds” would be less risky than their current fund.
“If there’s an economic crash tomorrow, the chances of you losing a big chunk of your super are quite high (in your existing fund). But if it’s spread over a more professional fund, one of the big bank funds or something like that, they’ve got access to between 600 and 1000 different investment options,” the cold caller said.
ASIC commissioner Alan Kirkland blasted lead generators for steering people to investment choices that would leave them worse off.
“Lead generation activities that involve finding people on social media or through unsolicited phone calls and ultimately convincing them to switch their super have no place in legitimate financial advice businesses,” Mr Kirkland told The Australian.
“Some lead generators are making misleading statements when they’re talking to members of the public. And some are doing things that should be done by financial advisers such as fact finding, risk profiling clients and discussing investment recommendations,” he said.
Lead generation, including cold calling, is a marketing tool designed to create interest in a product or service. That ‘lead’ can then be converted into a sale. Financial advisers pay lead generators for passing these tips on.
In some models reviewed by ASIC, the referral partner could receive up to 100 per cent of the client’s initial advice fee.
The regulator’s probe came after the Shield and First Guardian failures put a spotlight on dodgy tactics used by a segment of the advice industry. All up, about 12,000 people put $1bn of their super into the liquidated schemes, many after being contacted by cold callers.
The scandal pushed the regulator to name and shame dozens of advice firms using lead generators, including Clear Sky Financial, Limitless Wealth and Ready Advice.
The government, meanwhile, is pushing ahead with long-awaited financial advice reforms, including plans to ban unlicensed lead generators working in the advice industry.
But lobby group Super Consumers Australia said ASIC’s findings showed advice licensees could not be relied on to regulate the behaviour of lead generators.
“Giving these businesses a licence won’t change the financial incentives driving this behaviour,” Super Consumers chief executive Xavier O’Halloran said. “The government needs to ban lead generation for super switching and financial advice. People should be getting financial advice based on what’s best for them, not what earns a salesperson a payday.”
